entries.title: What is SousChef?
entries.summary: SousChef is a Household Food Operating System — not a recipe app. It tracks your pantry, learns your cooking patterns, plans meals from what you actually have, and builds a kitchen memory that compounds over time.
entries.keywords: What is SousChef?

entries.title: What happens when AI credits run out?
entries.summary: Your pantry, inventory, Brain insights, and deterministic features keep working. AI-heavy actions like meal plan generation pause until credits refresh — you are never locked out of your kitchen data. See our AI Usage Policy for credit costs.
entries.keywords: What happens when AI credits run out?

entries.title: Do you sell my food or shopping data?
entries.summary: No. SousChef learns your kitchen to serve you, not to sell you. We do not sell household food data, shopping habits, or family traditions. See our Privacy Policy for full detail.
entries.keywords: Do you sell my food or shopping data?

entries.title: Can my whole family share one kitchen?
entries.summary: Yes. Free supports up to 2 household members (join-only). Plus and Family support full Cook Together — shared pantry, Brain, and cook logs. Family tier includes priority AI responses.
entries.keywords: Can my whole family share one kitchen?

entries.title: Are nutrition estimates medical advice?
entries.summary: No. Per-serving nutrition on meal cards is an approximate estimate from ingredient references — not medical, dietary, or food safety advice. Always verify allergens, portions, and expiration dates yourself.
entries.keywords: Are nutrition estimates medical advice?

entries.title: Can I export or delete my data?
entries.summary: Yes. Access, export, and delete your kitchen data via Settings or by emailing hello@homechef.ai. Account deletion includes a 7-day grace period before permanent removal.
entries.keywords: Can I export or delete my data?

entries.title: When does paid billing start?
entries.summary: Core product is live and free during beta. Stripe billing for Plus ($9/mo) and Family ($18/mo) activates at launch — full access now so you can prove the loop before paying. No surprise AI overage charges.
entries.keywords: When does paid billing start?

entries.title: Who is Clara?
entries.summary: Clara is your Sous Chef — the intelligence layer that reads your pantry, explains why a meal fits, coaches techniques, and remembers what your household keeps or replaces. Basic pantry Q&A uses zero credits.
entries.keywords: Who is Clara?

entries.title: How do I learn about features before signing up?
entries.summary: Press ⌘K (or Ctrl+K) on any marketing page to search the site or ask questions about SousChef. For your personal pantry and meal plans, sign in to the app.

entries.title: Casserole
entries.summary: One-dish baked comfort — French word, Midwest soul.
entries.keywords: dish casserole hot dish Depression-era and WWII rationing made one-dish meals practical. 1950s freezer marketing cemented tuna noodle and green bean formats. Modern remakes often deconstruct; originals were engineered for cans and convenience.

entries.title: Chili
entries.summary: Texas-born stew of meat and chiles — beans debate included.
entries.keywords: dish chili chilli chile con carne Chili spread via cattle trails and World's Fair booths (1893 Chicago). Canned chili (1920s) and chili powder blends made it a national pantry meal. Regional forks include Cincinnati five-way, New Mexico green chile stew, and vegetarian bean-heavy bowls far from Lone

entries.title: Green Bean Casserole
entries.summary: 1955 Campbell's test kitchen invention — America's Thanksgiving side dish.
entries.keywords: dish green bean casserole bean casserole The recipe card debuted in 1955 and became a Thanksgiving fixture by the 1960s. entries.title: Grain Bowl
entries.summary: 2000s café format — ancient grains meet modern macro bowls.
entries.keywords: dish quinoa bowl grain bowl power bowl buddha bowl Instagram-era food photography made bowls visual shorthand for "healthy." Quinoa bowls specifically rode the 2013 UN Year of Quinoa and wellness trend. Home versions are essentially intentional leftovers — a format, not a fixed recipe.

entries.title: BBQ Sauce
entries.summary: American condiment family — sweet Kansas City to vinegar Carolina to pepper Texas.
entries.keywords: ingredient bbq sauce barbecue sauce Commercial bottled sauce took off after WWII when suburban grills met supermarket convenience. entries.title: Black Beans
entries.summary: New World legume — backbone of Latin American, Caribbean, and Southern bowls.
entries.keywords: ingredient black bean turtle bean Archaeological evidence places bean cultivation at roughly 7,000 years old in the Americas. entries.title: Chicken Breast
entries.summary: Lean poultry cut — America's default weeknight protein since the 1980s.
entries.keywords: ingredient chicken breast chicken Before industrial farming, older stewing hens and flavorful dark meat ruled home kitchens. Broiler revolution (1940s–60s) made chicken cheaper than beef. Skinless breast became a health-food icon in the 1980s–90s despite being easier to overcook than thighs.

entries.title: Garlic
entries.summary: Central Asian allium — global flavor base for 5,000+ years.
entries.keywords: ingredient garlic Garlic traveled the Silk Road and Columbian exchange routes until it appeared in nearly every major cuisine. Louis Pasteur documented its antibacterial properties in 1858. Modern research focuses on allicin — the compound released when cloves are crushed.

entries.title: Quinoa
entries.summary: Andean seed prized for complete protein — not a true grain.
entries.keywords: ingredient quinoa Quinoa sustained high-altitude civilizations for millennia before Spanish colonization disrupted its cultivation in favor of wheat. entries.title: White Rice
entries.summary: Domesticated grass seed — feeds half the planet.
entries.keywords: ingredient white rice rice Rice terracing spread through Southeast Asia; Islamic trade brought it to Spain and then the Americas. Carolina Gold rice made Charleston wealthy in the 1700s. Modern enrichment (vitamins added back to milled rice) began in the U.S. in the 1940s to prevent deficiency disea

entries.title: Texas Brisket
entries.summary: Central Texas pit tradition — salt, pepper, smoke, time.
entries.keywords: style brisket texas bbq smoked brisket Aaron Franklin and the Austin barbecue boom (2000s–2010s) turned brisket into a national pilgrimage food. Purist rub is often just salt and coarse pepper (Dalmatian rub). Sauce on the side, if at all — the meat is the point.

entries.title: Braise
entries.summary: Sear then simmer covered in liquid — transforms tough cuts.
entries.keywords: technique braise braised slow cook Escoffier codified braising in French repertoire; American Dutch oven and slow-cooker adaptations made it weeknight-accessible. Collagen breaks down around 160–180°F over time — the science behind fork-tender pot roast.

entries.title: Roux
entries.summary: Equal fat + flour cooked together — Louisiana gravies and French mother sauces.
entries.keywords: technique roux Roux-thickened sauces define French classical cuisine and Gulf Coast cooking alike. Cajun dark roux can take 45+ minutes of stirring — a ritual, not a shortcut. Instant roux products appeared in Louisiana groceries in the late 1900s for weeknight gumbo.

entries.title: Sunday Chili
entries.summary: American weekend ritual — low simmer while life happens elsewhere.
entries.keywords: tradition sunday chili game day chili Post-WWII suburban life cemented "Sunday dinner" as family anchor. Chili powder marketing (Gebhardt, Mexene) made Texas-style stew doable in Ohio kitchens by 1920. Game-day chili cook-offs became charity fundraisers nationwide from the 1970s onward.
